---
title: "Deviance"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

We begin with two observed SuperTelicity rows, one *in* response and one *for* response:

```{r}
#| label: observed-saturated-rows
#| echo: true
st <- read.csv("data/supertelicity/supertelicity-cloze.csv")
observed_saturated_rows <- st[c(
  which(st$prep_in == 1L)[[1L]],
  which(st$prep_in == 0L)[[1L]]
), c("participant_id", "sentence_id", "verb", "verb_type", "preposition", "prep_in")]
observed_saturated_rows
```

The best possible fit to these two rows would assign probability one to each observed response. It would use a separate fitted probability for each row, so it would reproduce the data exactly. We call this unrestricted benchmark the **saturated model**.

Our regression model usually imposes restrictions: two rows with the same predictors receive the same fitted probability, and a coefficient determines how probabilities change across predictor values. The fitted regression will thus give the observed outcomes less probability than the saturated benchmark. **Deviance** is twice the difference between their maximized log likelihoods. Smaller deviance means that the fitted model has lost less log likelihood relative to the exact-fit benchmark.

The likelihood definition comes from [maximum likelihood](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd): observed outcomes are fixed while parameter values vary. An [event](../foundations/possibilities-and-events.qmd) determines which response occurred, [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) licenses the rowwise product, and a [residual](residuals.qmd) subtracts the fitted response from the observed response on a chosen scale. Deviance aggregates likelihood discrepancies rather than raw residual squares.

We first define the saturated comparison, then connect deviance differences to nested models, and finally separate training fit from held-out predictive performance.

$$
D=2\{\ell_{\mathrm{sat}}-\ell(\widehat\theta)\}.
$$

This definition follows the likelihood ratio construction from [maximum likelihood](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd). For the two observed Bernoulli rows above, a saturated model sets $\widehat\pi_1=1$ and $\widehat\pi_2=0$, so

$$
\ell_{\mathrm{sat}}
=
\log(1)+\log(1)=0.
$$

For any nonsaturated fitted probabilities $0<\widehat\pi_i<1$,

$$
\ell(\widehat{\boldsymbol\pi})
=
\sum_i
\left[
y_i\log\widehat\pi_i
+(1-y_i)\log(1-\widehat\pi_i)
\right]
\leq 0.
$$

For Bernoulli rows, the saturated contribution is zero, so residual deviance is $-2\ell(\widehat\theta)$. We compare four population models for the same SuperTelicity rows.

```{r}
#| label: fit-deviance-sequence
#| echo: true
st$verb_type <- factor(st$verb_type, levels = c("manner", "result"))
st$contentfulness <- factor(st$contentfulness,
                            levels = c("contentful", "bleached", "templatic"))
models <- list(
  intercept = glm(prep_in ~ 1, binomial(), st),
  verb_type = glm(prep_in ~ verb_type, binomial(), st),
  additive = glm(prep_in ~ verb_type + contentfulness, binomial(), st),
  interaction = glm(prep_in ~ verb_type * contentfulness, binomial(), st)
)
comparison <- data.frame(
  model = factor(names(models), levels = names(models)),
  parameters = vapply(models, function(x) length(coef(x)), integer(1)),
  residual_deviance = vapply(models, deviance, numeric(1))
)
comparison$deviance_reduction <- c(NA, -diff(comparison$residual_deviance))
comparison
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-deviance-sequence
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(comparison, aes(model, residual_deviance, group = 1)) +
  geom_line(color = "#1F5A85") + geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Residual deviance") + theme_classic()
```

For nested models fit to identical rows with the same family, the deviance difference is

$$
\Delta D=2\{\ell(\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{larger}})-
\ell(\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{smaller}})\}.
$$

It is a likelihood ratio statistic under the usual regularity conditions. The sequence shows how much each added structure improves fit to the rows. It does not correct repeated participant and sentence dependence, and comparisons across different response families or different row sets generally do not have this interpretation.

If the smaller model has $p_0$ free coefficients and the larger nested model has $p_1$, the reference degrees of freedom are $p_1-p_0$. Under interior parameters, identifiable models, independent rows, and a sufficiently regular large-sample approximation,

$$
\Delta D\overset{\cdot}{\sim}\chi^2_{p_1-p_0}
$$

when the smaller restriction generates the data. This is the same asymptotic argument developed for [likelihood-ratio tests](../model-criticism-and-prediction/likelihood-ratio-tests.qmd). A smaller deviance establishes better in-sample likelihood for the nested comparison. It does not establish that the larger model is scientifically adequate.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Why is the saturated Bernoulli log likelihood zero?
2. When does a deviance difference equal a likelihood-ratio statistic?
3. Does a large deviance reduction repair repeated-participant dependence?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Each fitted probability equals its observed zero or one, so every observed outcome receives probability one and log probability zero. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->
2. The models must be nested, use the same observations and likelihood family, and be compared at their maximum likelihood estimates. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->
3. No. The comparison still uses the declared likelihood for individual rows and inherits its dependence assumptions. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->

</details>
